power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Observational studies sometimes report that individual medications are associated with lower mortality, but such signals are rarely compared across drugs and health systems.

We screened prescription medications for associations with all-cause mortality using timedependent Cox models in six cohorts from the UK, US, Finland, Hong Kong and Japan (8.93 million individuals aged 40 years or older; 1.49 billion prescriptions).
Most medications were associated with higher mortality, reflecting confounding by indication.

A few medications showed inverse associations with mortality, notably the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) vaccine, the antimalarials atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) and mefloquine, and the hormone replacement therapy estradiol.
These associations were only modestly attenuated by adjustment for comorbidity, lifestyle and socio-economic factors, and persisted within strata defined by pre-existing disease.
While adjustment for self-reported health abolished the Malarone association, probably reflecting a healthy traveler profile, the VZV association was maintained.
In FinnGen, deaths from external causes, which vaccination cannot prevent, were lower among VZV vaccine users, but much less so than all-cause mortality.

In a target trial emulation in All of Us, the VZV association was maintained against matched unvaccinated individuals (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.53-0.70) and pneumococcal vaccine recipients (HR 0.64, 0.55-0.74), but was attenuated against recipients of tetanus-diphtheria vaccines, a group that also has low mortality (HR 0.85, 0.70-1.03).
Healthy-user selection contributes to these signals but does not appear to fully explain the VZV vaccine association, which warrants confirmation in randomized trials.
This multinational atlas provides a resource for prioritizing drug-repurposing candidates in ageing research.
Population ageing has intensified interest in whether existing medications influence survival beyond their primary indication 1, 2 .
text.formatted: Population ageing has intensified interest in whether existing medications influence survival beyond their primary indication <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Observational studies have reported such associations for individual drugs 3 , but each typically examines a single agent in a single health system, with study-specific designs and covariates.
text.formatted: Observational studies have reported such associations for individual drugs <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> , but each typically examines a single agent in a single health system, with study-specific designs and covariates.

text.text: This makes it dicicult to judge whether a given signal is reproducible, or how it compares with the many medications never examined.

Several such signals have later failed to replicate in randomized trials, hormone replacement therapy being the best-known example 4, 5 , largely because of confounding by indication, immortal time bias and healthy-user bias [6] [7] [8] .
text.formatted: Several such signals have later failed to replicate in randomized trials, hormone replacement therapy being the best-known example <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> , largely because of confounding by indication, immortal time bias and healthy-user bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> .

text.text: Real-world data (RWD) from electronic health records and population biobanks now make it possible to examine many medications simultaneously 9 .
text.formatted: Real-world data (RWD) from electronic health records and population biobanks now make it possible to examine many medications simultaneously <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: Such a screen cannot establish causal ecects, but it can serve three purposes: mapping drug-mortality associations under a single pipeline; testing whether specific signals replicate across health systems with dicerent prescribing practices; and characterizing how sensitive each signal is to adjustment for comorbidity, lifestyle and selfreported health, that is, how much of it is plausibly explained by who receives the drug.

To address this knowledge gap, we developed a multinational pharmacoepidemiology framework to systematically evaluate the association between prescription drug utilization and all-cause mortality, leveraging six independent cohorts spanning three continents.

Our investigation integrates harmonized longitudinal data from the All of Us 10 (AOU) Research Program and the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 11 (NHANES) in the United States; the UK Biobank 12 (UKBB) and FinnGen 13 in Europe; alongside the Hong Kong territorywide EHR database (Clinical Data Analysis and Reporting System 14 ; CDARS) and the Japan Medical Data Center 15 (JMDC) claims database in Asia.
text.formatted: Our investigation integrates harmonized longitudinal data from the All of Us 10 (AOU) Research Program and the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> (NHANES) in the United States; the UK Biobank <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> (UKBB) and FinnGen <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> in Europe; alongside the Hong Kong territorywide EHR database (Clinical Data Analysis and Reporting System <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> ; CDARS) and the Japan Medical Data Center <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> (JMDC) claims database in Asia.

text.text: This trans-continental integration captures a cross-section of global prescribing practices, sociodemographic profiles, and healthcare infrastructures.
To examine survival outcomes while mitigating temporal biases, we applied time-dependent covariate 16 (TDC) Cox proportional hazards models across the prescribed drug catalog.
text.formatted: To examine survival outcomes while mitigating temporal biases, we applied time-dependent covariate <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> (TDC) Cox proportional hazards models across the prescribed drug catalog.

text.text: We utilized a stepwise adjustment pipeline: beginning with baseline demographic adjustments (age, sex and enrollment year), followed by clinical risk adjustments utilizing the Charlson Comorbidity Index 17 (CCI), and concluding with adjustments for lifestyle and socioeconomic factors, including smoking status, body mass index (BMI) and socio-economic status (SES).
text.formatted: We utilized a stepwise adjustment pipeline: beginning with baseline demographic adjustments (age, sex and enrollment year), followed by clinical risk adjustments utilizing the Charlson Comorbidity Index <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> (CCI), and concluding with adjustments for lifestyle and socioeconomic factors, including smoking status, body mass index (BMI) and socio-economic status (SES).

text.text: Lastly, to determine whether increased survival is maintained in dicerent clinical contexts, we conducted stratified analyses across sex and major clinical subgroups (e.g., isolating ecects within oncology or diabetology cohorts versus relatively healthy baselines).

Finally, to probe healthy-user bias directly, we examined a negative-control exposure that shares the selection profile of a candidate drug but has no plausible ecect on mortality, and cause-specific mortality outcomes that the drugs cannot plausibly acect.
For the VZV vaccine, we additionally emulated a target trial 18 , comparing vaccinees with unvaccinated individuals and with recipients of other adult vaccines.
text.formatted: For the VZV vaccine, we additionally emulated a target trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> , comparing vaccinees with unvaccinated individuals and with recipients of other adult vaccines.

text.text: We present the resulting atlas as an openly available, hypothesis-generating resource to help prioritize candidates for drug repurposing and further study.

Its associations are not estimates of causal drug ecects: inverse associations ultimately require drug-specific randomized trials, before they can inform practice, and importantly, associations with higher mortality should not be read as evidence of harm.
We harmonized longitudinal data from six population cohorts, together encompassing 8.93 million individuals and 1.49 billion prescriptions (Table 1).
text.formatted: We harmonized longitudinal data from six population cohorts, together encompassing 8.93 million individuals and 1.49 billion prescriptions (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: The cohorts differed widely in design and clinical profile, spanning population biobanks with deep phenotyping (UKBB, FinnGen, AOU), a nationally representative survey (NHANES), a territory-wide hospital database of older adults (CDARS) and an insurance claims database of working-age adults and their dependants (JMDC).

Accordingly, mean age at enrollment ranged from 52 years in JMDC to 68 years in CDARS, median follow-up from 3.4 years in AOU to 14.7 years in UKBB, and the proportion of participants who died during follow-up from 0.4% in JMDC to 29.5% in CDARS.
This heterogeneity in populations, healthcare systems and data capture provides a stringent test of whether drug-mortality associations replicate across settings.

To capture the dynamic nature of drug exposure and minimize immortal time bias, we employed a time-dependent covariate (TDC) survival analysis utilizing Cox proportional hazards models (Figure 1, S1).
text.formatted: To capture the dynamic nature of drug exposure and minimize immortal time bias, we employed a time-dependent covariate (TDC) survival analysis utilizing Cox proportional hazards models (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: This framework allowed us to evaluate the hazard ratios (HR) for all-cause mortality associated with specific prescription medications with progressive adjustment for baseline comorbidities, in subjects aged 40yo or older.
We first evaluated and meta-analyzed these associations in a first model (Model 1), adjusted for sex, age and year of enrollment.

Pooled estimates combined AOU, UKBB, FinnGen and CDARS; NHANES, which only captured medication use at baseline, and JMDC, which comprised over 80% of all participants and would dominate pooled estimates, are shown at the cohort level but were not pooled (Methods).
In this model, most medications were associated with higher mortality (HR > 1; Figure 2A).
text.formatted: In this model, most medications were associated with higher mortality (HR > 1; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2A</ref>).

text.text: This is the expected pattern when users are compared with all non-users: medications are prescribed to people with the conditions they treat, and those conditions, rather than the drugs, carry the excess risk (confounding by indication).
These HRs should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of harm.
Against this background, a small number of medications were associated with lower mortality across cohorts.

These include notably the Shingles (VZV) vaccine, the DTP vaccine and the antimalarials atovaquone/proguanil (Malarone) and mefloquine, which remained significant after Bonferroni correction (Figure 2B).
text.formatted: These include notably the Shingles (VZV) vaccine, the DTP vaccine and the antimalarials atovaquone/proguanil (Malarone) and mefloquine, which remained significant after Bonferroni correction (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref>).

text.text: Typhoid vaccine (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.43-1.09), tibolone (HR 0.71, 0.44-1.15) and estradiol (HR 0.77, 0.63-0.94) also showed inverse associations of similar magnitude.

To further characterize these associations, we conducted sex-specific analyses adjusted for baseline age and enrollment year ("Model 1"), which showed that the lower mortality association for most medications was maintained across both male and female populations (Figure 2C).
text.formatted: To further characterize these associations, we conducted sex-specific analyses adjusted for baseline age and enrollment year ("Model 1"), which showed that the lower mortality association for most medications was maintained across both male and female populations (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2C</ref>).

text.text: Lower mortality, sex-agnostic signals were observed for prophylactic immunizations, including the VZV (varicella-zoster) vaccine and the DTP vaccine, as well as the antimalarial combination of atovaquone/proguanil alongside mefloquine.
Hormone therapies (estradiol, tibolone) were, as expected, prescribed almost exclusively to women.
To reduce confounding factors, we applied further adjustments to our base model (Figure 2D).
text.formatted: To reduce confounding factors, we applied further adjustments to our base model (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2D</ref>).

text.text: We then looked at mortality associations adjusted for baseline CCI ("Model 2"), as well as lifestyle and socioeconomic factors ("Model 3"), including smoking status, BMI, and SES, measured using the Townsend deprivation index (UK Biobank only).

With Model 2 and Model 3, the inverse associations were only modestly attenuated (Shingles vaccine HR 0.44 in Model 1 and 0.45 in Model 3; DTP vaccine 0.72 and 0.74; Malarone 0.61 and 0.67; estradiol 0.77 and 0.81).

In contrast, atorvastatin and rosuvastatin, statins that reduce all-cause mortality in randomized trials 19 , were not associated with lower mortality in any model, and adjustment for comorbidity moved their HRs from above 1 towards the null (atorvastatin 1.35 to 1.14; rosuvastatin 1.10 to 0.98; Figure 2F), consistent with confounding by indication rather than an absence of benefit.

text.text: To determine if these lower mortality associations persisted within inherently high-risk or biologically vulnerable patient subpopulations, we conducted stratified analyses based on specific pre-existing clinical conditions, including cancer, circulatory disease (CVD), and diabetes, and behavioral stratification based on smoking status (Figure 2E).

We also evaluated these medications within a relatively "healthy" patient sub-cohort, devoid of such comorbidities.
Within this relatively healthier stratum, the inverse associations were generally maintained; for the Shingles vaccine, the pooled estimate became imprecise (HR 0.51, 95% CI 0.23-1.15).

Lastly, to reduce confounding by indication and healthy-user bias, we compared the medications with the strongest inverse associations against active comparators sharing their indication or preventive context (selection criteria in Methods; Figure S2).
text.formatted: Lastly, to reduce confounding by indication and healthy-user bias, we compared the medications with the strongest inverse associations against active comparators sharing their indication or preventive context (selection criteria in Methods; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">S2</ref>).

text.text: Compared with other adult vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal), the VZV and DTP vaccines remained associated with lower mortality.
Estradiol was associated with lower mortality relative to estriol, but not relative to tibolone or conjugated estrogens.
We next examined whether the strongest inverse associations could reflect the characteristics of drug users rather than drug effects (Figure 3).
text.formatted: We next examined whether the strongest inverse associations could reflect the characteristics of drug users rather than drug effects (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Malarone users reported markedly better health than users of the DTP and Shingles vaccines and than the overall cohort (Figure 3A), and adjustment attenuated the Malarone association towards the null, whereas the Shingles and DTP vaccine associations were largely maintained (Figure 3B).

In this large-scale, multi-national analysis, we systematically evaluated the association between prescription medications and all-cause mortality across six diverse populationbased cohorts.

Our results identify several pharmacological classes associated with lower all-cause mortality, building upon and extending our previous findings that evaluated prescribed medications in the UK Biobank 22 .

text.text: The current investigation deployed a timedependent covariate (TDC) framework to minimize immortal time bias and capture the dynamic nature of drug exposure.

Despite these methodological dicerences, our current cross-national analysis confirms the previously observed lower-mortality associations for medications such as estradiol, replicating these associations across multiple, independent healthcare systems and demographics.

By combining six cohorts from three continents in a common analytical pipeline, and by probing healthy-user bias with complementary negative-control analyses, this work provides a framework for distinguishing robust drugmortality signals from selection ecects.
Two features of the design are important for interpreting the atlas.
First, because each medication is compared with all non-users, many associations reflect confounding by indication.

HRs above 1 largely index the severity of the treated condition, and the absence of an inverse association does not imply absence of benefit: statins, which reduce all-cause mortality in randomized trials 19 , appear null here.

text.text: Second, the inverse associations that stand out against this background are concentrated in preventive and elective treatments (vaccines, travel prophylaxis and hormone therapy), the categories most susceptible to healthy-user bias 8 .

text.text: The atlas should therefore be read as a ranked set of signals, together with their sensitivity to adjustment, rather than as estimates of drug ecects.

A well-recognized challenge in observational pharmacoepidemiology is healthy-user bias 8 , wherein patients prescribed certain preventive therapies generally exhibit healthier baseline behaviors, better healthcare access, and higher socioeconomic status.

text.text: For example, the antimalarial combination atovaquone/proguanil (Malarone), associated with lower mortality, may reflect a "healthy traveler ecect," as individuals receiving prophylactic travel medications inherently possess the physical capacity, financial resources, and overall health required to undertake international travel.
Other medications may also be subject to this bias, including vaccines and HRT.
We probed this bias through stepwise adjustment for the CCI, lifestyle factors and self-reported health, and through stratification within highly morbid populations.
These attenuated but did not abolish the associations.
Still, residual healthy-user bias cannot be excluded.
Some additional observations support this interpretation.

Typhoid vaccine, which shares the traveler profile of Malarone but cannot plausibly reduce mortality, showed an inverse association of similar magnitude; Malarone users reported better self-rated health, and adjustment for it attenuated the Malarone association.
For the Shingles vaccine, deaths from external causes and falls, which the vaccine cannot prevent, were also lower among users, but much less so than all-cause mortality.

In a target trial emulation in AOU, the association was maintained against unvaccinated individuals and pneumococcal vaccine recipients but attenuated against recipients of Td/Tdap vaccines, and mortality curves separated soon after vaccination, when a protective ecect is unlikely.
The inverse association of the DTP vaccine itself points the same way.
Yet when calibrated against DTP or Td/Tdap vaccines, which share this selection, a modest VZV association of roughly 15-25% lower mortality remained, compatible with a smaller true ecect.
Healthy-user selection therefore contributes to this association, but the residual association could reflect a true protective ecect, which warrants evaluation in randomized trials.
Hormone replacement therapy (HRT), specifically estradiol, was associated with lower mortality in women aged 40 years or older (HR 0.77), with a similar but imprecise estimate for tibolone.

These findings are consistent with prior reports showing benefits of estrogen maintenance on cardiovascular, bone, and metabolic health in the post-menopausal period 23 , but contrast with the trials of the Women's Health Initiative (WHI), which did not support HRT for the prevention of cardiovascular and other chronic diseases 4,5 .

text.text: Our estimates are, however, not directly comparable with the WHI.

The trials tested oral conjugated equine estrogens, alone or combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate, in women aged 50-79 years who were on average more than a decade past menopause and mostly free of menopausal symptoms, with the aim of preventing chronic disease.

Current practice, and most prescriptions captured here, instead involve 17β-estradiol, frequently administered transdermally and combined with micronized progesterone, and initiated near menopause for symptom relief.

In WHI analyses stratified by age, women who started HRT at 50-59 years had lower all-cause mortality during the intervention phase 4 , consistent with the hypothesis that the timing of initiation matters.

text.text: A particularly notable finding was the association between vaccination with the varicellazoster virus (VZV) vaccine and lower all-cause mortality.

The lower mortality association observed for vaccines, and particularly the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) vaccine, aligns with recent evidence showing a decreased risk of developing neurodegenerative disease.

Recent experiments have shown that both the live attenuated and recombinant shingles vaccines significantly reduce the subsequent risk of developing dementia, with the recombinant formulation yielding a substantial increase in dementia-free time [24] [25] [26] .

It was, however, robust to adjustment for comorbidity, lifestyle and self-rated health, and was maintained against unvaccinated individuals and pneumococcal vaccine recipients, suggesting that healthy-user selection contributes to, but may not fully explain, it.
Metformin users did not show lower mortality than non-users in our data, consistent with reports that metformin may not extend lifespan compared with non-diabetic controls 29, 30 .

Subsequent longitudinal studies may investigate the temporal trajectories of comorbidities, or intrinsic capacity 35 and frailty in patients prescribed these agents.

text.text: Determining whether therapies like HRT, and the zoster vaccine are also associated with lower morbidity and higher functional capacity in old age will be essential to determine the potential benefit of these drugs.
There are several other limitations to this study.
First, patients were considered continuously exposed following their first prescription, reflecting an intent-to-treat 37 (ITT) analog approach.

This assumption may inflate lower mortality associations for one-oc preventive interventions such as vaccines and antimalarial prophylaxis, while separately biasing acute short-course drugs such as antibiotics.
For NHANES since medication data was only available at baseline, the time-to-drug was set to 0.
Thus, NHANES contributed a baselineexposure (prevalent-user) analysis, which is more susceptible to immortal-time and prevalent-user biases.
Throughout, we describe medications as associated with lower mortality; given the observational design, these associations should not be interpreted as causal ecects.
In addition, some drug exposure may have been missed including medications bought over the counter, or given outside the recording system (for example, vaccinations given in pharmacies).
Furthermore, the integrated healthcare databases carry structural and clinical heterogeneity.
The six cohorts encompass fundamentally distinct data capture environments, spanning routine primary care to tertiary hospital settings.
For instance, datasets such as the UK Biobank and the JMDC predominantly capture community-based, general practice (GP) outpatient prescriptions.
In contrast, comprehensive EHR systems like CDARS and FinnGen incorporate a substantial volume of inpatient, hospital-administered therapeutics.

Because JMDC is substantially larger than the other cohorts and NHANES captured only baseline (prevalent) medication use, both were excluded from the pooled estimates and are reported at the cohort level only.
Lastly, target trial emulation was performed in a single cohort (AOU) with limited follow-up.

We also attempted an emulation for estradiol, among women aged 45-59 years initiating systemic estradiol compared with initiators of vaginal estrogen, but the number of deaths in this age range was too low for an informative estimate.
In conclusion, this multinational atlas maps the associations between prescription medications and all-cause mortality across six cohorts on three continents.

Most associations reflect the clinical context in which drugs are prescribed, but a small number of preventive medications, most notably the VZV vaccine, showed consistent inverse associations that were robust to conventional adjustment and, for the VZV vaccine, largely maintained in a target trial emulation, although attenuation against a comparable vaccine group suggests that healthy-user selection contributes to them.
These signals warrant confirmation in randomized trials.

Together with the cohort-level and pooled estimates made available with this work, these results provide a resource for prioritizing candidates for drug repurposing in ageing research and for designing confirmatory studies.
We conducted a multinational, retrospective, longitudinal cohort study using RWD from six independent, large-scale population biobanks and EHR databases spanning three continents.
The integrated data sources from the United States included the AOU and the NHANES.
European cohorts comprised the UK Biobank and the FinnGen study.
Asian cohorts included the CDARS, representing the territory-wide public healthcare system of Hong Kong, alongside the JMDC claims database from Japan.

A federated analytical approach was employed wherein standardized analytical scripts were executed locally within each cohort's secure environment, and summary-level statistics were subsequently meta-analyzed.
The analysis plan was not preregistered.
This work complies with all relevant ethical regulations.
A full list of the ethics boards that approved the study protocols is provided at the end of this section.
The AOU 10 is a highly diverse United States initiative that integrates electronic health records, survey responses, and biospecimen data.
It specifically focuses on historically underrepresented populations, providing comprehensive longitudinal health tracking for over 500,000 participants.
The medication screen used Curated Data Repository (CDR) release R2025Q4R6.
The NHANES 11 provides a nationally representative US sample through extensive clinical, nutritional, and laboratory examinations.
These cross-sectional baseline assessments are subsequently linked to longitudinal Medicare and mortality records to evaluate long-term health outcomes.

Medication data was available for around 200,000 individuals.
It features deep phenotypic profiling, including genetic, lifestyle, and physical measurements, comprehensively linked to ongoing national electronic health records.

The FINNGEN 13 study (release 13) is a nationwide initiative that combines comprehensive genomic profiles with decades of longitudinal electronic health registry data for approximately 500,000 Finnish citizens. 350,000 individuals with medication and mortality available were included in the study.
The CDARS 14 is a territory-wide EHR database managed by the Hospital Authority (HA) of Hong Kong.
The HA is the sole public healthcare provider that manages 43 hospitals and institutions and 123 outpatient clinics in Hong Kong, covering >80% of all hospital admissions.

text.text: The base population for each cohort included adult individuals aged 40yo or older.

The index date ("time-zero") was defined as the date of study entry or baseline assessment within each respective cohort, while in FinnGen the index date was defined as the date of first prescription record.
Individuals with missing data for critical baseline demographic variables, such as age and sex, or whose death was recorded on or before their index date were excluded from the analytical cohort.
Drug exposure data were curated and harmonised through a combination of automated coding and manual review, tailored to the source nomenclature of each cohort.

For UKBB, AOU, NHANES, and CDARS, drug names were extracted from free-text or proprietary fields and manually curated to resolve brand-name/generic equivalences, spelling variants, and multi-ingredient product names, mapping each entry to a single active principle.
For JMDC, standardised drug names were already available in the source data and required no additional curation.
For FINNGEN, drugs were identified and classified using Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) codes.

Following cohort-level curation, all drug names were harmonised across the six cohorts into a single unified nomenclature based on active ingredient, enabling direct cross-cohort comparisons of individual drugs and drug classes.
To ensure analytical stability, only drugs prescribed to more than 100 subjects within a given cohort were retained for analysis.
The primary exposure of interest was the utilization of prescription medications.
To mitigate immortal time bias, prescription drug exposure was modeled as a time-dependent covariate.
Follow-up time for all individuals contributed to the unexposed risk period until the date of their first incident prescription for a given drug or drug class.
From the date of the first prescription onward, their subsequent follow-up time was transitioned to the exposed risk period.
Individuals whose first recorded prescription preceded the index date were classified as exposed from the index date onward (prevalent users).
Patients were considered continuously exposed following their initial prescription, reflecting an intent-totreat analog approach.
Dose and duration of use were not modelled, and each drug was analysed separately against all individuals not (yet) exposed to it, without adjustment for comedication.
For NHANES, since medication data was only available at baseline, the timeto-drug was set to 0, and the same model was used otherwise.
JMDC patients were censored after age 75.
The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality.
Mortality status and the exact date of death were ascertained through linkage to national and regional death registries specific to each cohort.
These included the National Death Index for the United States cohorts, the NHS Information Centre and central registries for the European cohorts, and the Hong Kong Death Registry for the CDARS.
For JMDC, death information was recorded in enrollment data.
Follow-up continued until the date of death, loss to follow-up or administrative censoring (end of study period), whichever occurred first.
In FinnGen, the underlying cause of death was obtained from the national cause-of-death registry (Statistics Finland), coded according to ICD-10.
To control for confounding by indication and baseline health status, a comprehensive set of covariates was extracted and harmonized across the six databases.
Demographic variables included age at the index date, biological sex and enrollment date.
Comorbidity burden was quantified using the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), which was calculated for each patient using baseline diagnostic codes recorded before or at the index date.
In UKBB, for which individual-level data could not be re-accessed at the time of this analysis, the CCI was approximated by the sum of baseline circulatory disease, diabetes and cancer (range 0-3).
Furthermore, where available within specific cohorts, lifestyle and socioeconomic determinants were extracted.
These included BMI, smoking status (categorized as never, former, or current), and harmonized indices of socioeconomic status such as the Townsend index (UKBB only).
When the data was missing for whole variables (for ex.
BMI, and smoking status in CDARS) the respective cohorts were excluded from the sub-analyses using these variables.
In general the Cox was fitted only on complete cases.

In AOU, self-rated general health (excellent, very good, good, fair or poor) from the participant surveys was additionally available and was used in a sensitivity analysis adjusting Model 1 for this variable.

To evaluate the association between prescription medication and all-cause mortality while rigorously accounting for immortal time bias, we employed a time-dependent covariate survival analysis framework utilizing Cox proportional hazards models (R survival package, tmerge, coxph functions).
The primary timescale for the survival analysis was defined as the time on study, calculated from the date of cohort enrollment to the date of death or rightcensoring.
Drug exposure was inherently modeled as a dynamic variable to reflect the realities of longitudinal patient care.
For each evaluated medication, the specific time to first exposure was calculated in years as the interval between the baseline enrollment date and the first recorded date of prescription issuance.
To execute this, we utilized a counting process approach, restructuring patient observation periods into distinct start and stop intervals.
Medication use was incorporated into the Cox proportional hazards models as a binary, time-varying covariate.

Under this analytical framework, an individual contributed unexposed person-time to the baseline cohort risk pool until the exact date of their first prescription, after which their subsequent follow-up time was classified as exposed.

To ensure the statistical stability and reliability of our hazard ratio estimates, a Cox model was only computed for a specific medication if there were at least 15 observed mortality events among the actively exposed patient subset.

For incident cancer, diabetes and heart disease in AOU (Figure 4A), the same time-dependent Cox model, adjusted for age and sex, was fitted with the first recorded diagnosis as the event, excluding individuals diagnosed before enrollment; adjusted cumulative event curves were derived for a woman of mean age with and without exposure.

text.text: We applied a progressively stringent series of adjustment models: "Model 1" was adjusted for age at enrollment, sex, and the year of enrollment, "Model 2" was further adjusted for CCI, and "Model 3" further incorporated smoking status, body mass index, and socioeconomic status.
We also conducted stratified analyses to evaluate medicationmortality associations within distinct, clinically relevant subpopulations.

Independent timedependent Cox models performed across patient strata defined by baseline circulatory disease (I00-I99), cancer (C00-C99), diabetes (E08-E13), and smoking status, as well as within an explicitly healthy sub-cohort entirely free of these major underlying comorbidities.

Finally, to account for multiple testing, for each unique analytical scenario and model type, we applied Bonferroni correction, scaling the significance thresholds by the total number of evaluated drugs within that specific data subset.
To combine the cohort-specific hazard ratios, we conducted a random-effects metaanalysis across AOU, UKBB, FinnGen and CDARS.

NHANES, in which medication use was only recorded at baseline (prevalent users), and JMDC, which comprised over 80% of all participants and would dominate pooled estimates, were not pooled but are reported at the cohort level.
The meta-analysis was limited to medications that were evaluated in at least two of the pooled cohorts.
We pooled these individual cohort estimates utilizing the generic inverse variance method implemented via the rma function in the R metafor package.

Recognizing the inherent structural, demographic, and clinical heterogeneity across the global biobanks, we applied a random-effects model, estimating the between-study variance using the Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) method.
Meta-analysis p-values were Bonferroni-corrected for the number of drugs pooled within each analysis (e.g., 317 drugs in the main Model 1 analysis).
To reduce confounding by indication and healthy-user bias for the medications with the strongest inverse associations in the primary screen, we compared each with one or more active comparators.

Comparators were selected using the following criteria: (i) shared indication or use context: the comparator is prescribed for the same condition or in the same preventive setting (e.g., other vaccines routinely recommended for adults of the same age; other systemic estrogen formulations used for menopausal symptoms); (ii) comparable patient and prescriber profile: initiating either drug implies a similar level of healthcare engagement, so that healthy-user effects are expected to be shared; (iii) sufficient data: ≥100 new users and ≥15 deaths in at least two cohorts.
Applying these criteria, the comparators were: influenza and pneumococcal vaccines for the VZV and DTP vaccines; estriol, tibolone and conjugated estrogens for estradiol.

In a newuser active-comparator design, patients initiating drug A or drug B were followed from first initiation until death or end of follow-up, with Cox models estimating the HR for A versus B adjusted for age at initiation, sex, and time from cohort entry to initiation.

To probe healthy-user bias, we used typhoid vaccine as a negative-control exposure for atovaquone/proguanil: it is prescribed to the same population of international travelers but has no plausible effect on all-cause mortality in the populations studied.
Its association with mortality was estimated with the same time-dependent Cox models as all other drugs.
The DTP vaccine was interpreted in the same way for other adult vaccines.

In FinnGen, we additionally estimated cause-specific mortality for the Shingles vaccine and atovaquone/proguanil according to the underlying cause of death: external causes (ICD-10 V01-Y98), including falls (W00-W19), transport accidents (V01-V99) and suicide (X60-X84); cancer (C00-D48); and circulatory disease (I00-I99).
For each cause, deaths from that cause were treated as events and deaths from other causes were censored at the date of death (cause-specific hazards), using Model 1.
External causes served as negative-control outcomes that neither drug can plausibly prevent.
Estimates based on fewer than five deaths among exposed individuals are not reported.

Eligible individuals were aged 50-89 years, were enrolled in AOU, had at least one year of EHR history and at least one healthcare visit in the preceding two years, and had no prior record of zoster vaccination.
Time zero was the date of the first recorded zoster vaccine dose (live attenuated or recombinant), identified from drug and procedure records.
Only vaccinations after enrollment were included, to avoid immortal time between vaccination and enrollment.

Three comparator groups were used.

First, each vaccinee was matched on sex and birth year to up to five individuals who met the same eligibility criteria and were alive and unvaccinated on the vaccinee's vaccination date (risk-set sampling, equivalent to a sequence of trials, one per vaccination day); matched comparators shared the vaccinee's time zero.

Second and third, in new-user active-comparator designs, vaccinees were compared with individuals receiving a pneumococcal vaccine or a tetanus-diphtheria vaccine (Td or Tdap) who had no zoster vaccination on or before that date, with time zero at the comparator vaccination and the same eligibility criteria.
Individuals could contribute to both arms at different time zeros.
Confounding was addressed with propensity-score weights targeting the average treatment effect in the treated, truncated at the 99th percentile.

Propensity scores included age, calendar year, the Charlson Comorbidity Index and major comorbidities, the number of healthcare visit days and of distinct drugs in the previous two years, prior influenza vaccination, prior travel vaccines or antimalarials, smoking, education, BMI and self-rated health, all measured before time zero; active-comparator models additionally included sex and prior pneumococcal and Td/Tdap vaccination.
Balance was assessed with standardized mean differences (target <0.1).

Study design and analytical framework.
Overview of the multinational pharmacoepidemiology study evaluating the association between prescription medications and all-cause mortality.

The study integrated and harmonized longitudinal data from six population cohorts: UK Biobank (UKBB), All of Us (AOU), National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), Japan Medical Data Center (JMDC), Clinical Data Analysis and Reporting System (CDARS) and FinnGen.
A time-dependent covariate (TDC) survival analysis using Cox proportional hazards models was employed to mitigate immortal time bias.

The analytical pipeline included progressively stringent covariate adjustments (Models 1-3), stratified analyses by sex and pre-existing clinical conditions, and sensitivity analyses (active comparators, negative-control exposure and outcomes).
